case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Wisconsin TPR proceeds in two phases: grounds/unfitness, which the petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence and where partial summary judgment is available when no material fact is disputed, followed by a dispositional phase governed by the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the evidentiary threshold - clear and convincing evidence of an enumerated ground - that an agency finding must ultimately support in court.
key_cases.quote: A finding of parental unfitness is a necessary prerequisite to termination of parental rights, but a finding of unfitness does not necessitate that parental rights be terminated.

key_cases.holding: Wis. Stat. sec. 48.424(4), which requires a finding of unfitness once statutory grounds are proved, comports with substantive due process because the court retains discretion at disposition to dismiss the petition if termination is not warranted.
key_cases.relevance: It explains why a proven statutory ground compels an unfitness finding without offending due process.
key_cases.quote: The discretion that the statute vests in the court to dismiss the petition for termination if it finds termination is not warranted under the standards assures full, substantive due process.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal floor: an agency finding cannot support severance of parental rights on anything less than clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: The fundamental liberty interest of natural parents in the care, custody, and management of their child does not evaporate simply because they have not been model parents

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: Disclosure of an administrative 'indicated' child-abuse finding to employers deprives child care workers and career entrants of a protected liberty interest, entitling them to pre-indication notice and an opportunity to respond plus prompt post-deprivation review, while the agency may retain a 'credible evidence' standard that requires weighing exculpatory as well as inculpatory evidence; foster parents have no comparable career or property interest.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling circuit authority on the due process owed before an agency records a substantiated finding and puts it on a central register - the node Wisconsin case law leaves empty.
key_cases.quote: we believe that the imposition of this added legal impediment constitutes a very tangible loss of employment opportunities due to the disclosure of the indicated report

key_cases.case_name: State v. Bobby G. (In re Marquette S.)
key_cases.holding: In deciding whether a biological father failed to assume parental responsibility under Wis. Stat. sec. 48.415(6), the circuit court must consider the efforts he made after learning he is the father and before the grounds are adjudicated; the contrary partial summary judgment was reversed and the cause remanded for fact-finding.
key_cases.relevance: It limits what evidence a proven ground may rest on: a father's post-notice efforts count at the grounds phase, so an agency's early record cannot alone fix unfitness.
key_cases.quote: a circuit court must consider the biological father's efforts undertaken after he discovers that he is the father but before the circuit court adjudicates the grounds of the termination proceeding
